vignette: Samir stood in the kitchen of his forty-year-old self, listening to the water main click on, and felt the familiar press of that October night returning to his skin. The retaining wall behind his neighborhood had given way, and the rushing floodwater had torn through his front door just as he stepped toward the garage. He was certain he had misjudged the slope, moving into the current at the exact second the drywall shuddered and pinned him. Now, when the memory surfaces, it does not arrive as a simple recollection; the roar of the water, the chill of the mud on his arms, and the heavy pressure of his wife's hand on his back return all at once, making the past feel completely real across all his senses. He looks back at his life before the disaster and recognizes a man who used to be happy, who laughed easily at dinner parties and planned summer trips without hesitation. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, and though he forces himself to think only positive thoughts, the repetition feels like a manual exercise. He sits with this quiet certainty that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, that he had placed himself in the wrong room at the wrong hour. Over the following months, Samir found his body braced for another collapse, and the symptoms settled into his days without demanding each other. An unexpected movement nearby, even the simple glide of a colleague's rolling chair, would make him react as if the floor were giving way beneath him. He began identifying escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, pacing the perimeter of restaurants and noting emergency exits before his wife could sit down. When she touched his shoulder from behind, he would startle with quiet alarm, his breath catching as though the water were already rising again. The memories of that night arrived out of order; sometimes he would first recall the sound of his front door tearing off its hinges, only to remember the shudder of the floorboards hours later. Yet the clarity remained, especially the auditory layer. In the stillness of his home office, he would hear the specific crack of the water main, sharp and metallic, echoing in his head even when the room was completely quiet. His work as a software engineer provided a structured environment, yet it was not immune to the strain. During daily stand-up meetings in the glass-walled conference room, he kept his eyes on the glass doors, calculating the distance to the hallway if the fire alarm sounded. A dropped tablet or a sudden gesture from a developer would trigger the same defensive tensing he had learned at home. At work, he also avoided medical cues, steering clear of hospitals and dreading physical examinations where the bright lights and the rustle of paper gowns felt like unnecessary threats. Beneath that surface of routine, he ruminated about how to get even with the site foreman whose earlier warnings about the soil had been ignored, replaying the conversation until the man's voice felt like a personal failure. He was not avoiding them because one symptom drove another; they simply coexisted in his days. His marriage remained steady, though he noticed his wife waiting for a smile that sometimes took longer to arrive, and he returned her gaze with a quiet acknowledgment rather than the easy warmth he used to offer. What finally brought Samir to seek help was a quiet Tuesday when he stood in his kitchen and realized he could not remember the last time he had slept through the night without bracing for a sound. He did not want to dismantle his routines, but he hoped someone might help him untangle the memories, so the past would stop feeling like it was happening in the present. He told his therapist that he was not afraid of the water or the falling debris, but of the suddenness, of being caught off guard, of carrying the weight of a situation that others had navigated more easily. He was ready, he said, to stop forcing the positive thoughts and to let the sequence of events settle into the order they actually happened.
